topic: VPC Flow Logs and security group/NACL ACCEPT entries only confirm that traffic was permitted to leave the AWS side of a network path — they provide no visibility into whether packets successfully traverse hybrid connectivity (Direct Connect, Site-to-Site VPN, on-premises firewalls, or routing) to reach an on-premises destination. This is a hard troubleshooting pattern because every AWS-side signal looks correct (network layer accepted, IAM presumably fine), and the exam wants recognition that intermittent, unpatterned connectivity failures to an on-premises system point toward the hybrid network path itself (VPN/Direct Connect stability, intermediate firewalls, rate limiting) rather than any AWS-native access control layer.

question: A subscription box company's Athena-based reporting layer queries a 40 TB S3 data lake of order history, partitioned by order_year and order_month, stored as Snappy-compressed Parquet. The finance team runs the same monthly revenue-reconciliation query template each month, filtering to a single month's partition and scanning roughly 1.1 TB. Finance has just requested the ability to also run identical reconciliation logic against arbitrary custom date ranges spanning multiple months at a time, sometimes crossing year boundaries, without the platform team writing a new query for each request, while keeping the per-query cost predictable and avoiding accidental full-table scans if someone forgets to specify a date filter entirely. What combination of Athena features addresses both the flexible date-range requirement and the accidental-full-scan risk?
options: Create a parameterized Athena view over the partitioned table and grant finance direct console access, relying on analysts to remember a WHERE clause filtering order_year and order_month.
Convert the table from Athena-managed partitioning to Redshift Spectrum external tables, since Spectrum has no per-query cost at all regardless of scan volume.
Use Athena prepared statements for arbitrary date-range parameters, and set the workgroup's bytes-scanned control to auto-cancel any query, even an unfiltered one, past an approved threshold.

Disable Athena entirely for finance and require all reconciliation queries go through a Lambda function that hardcodes the date range server-side, preventing analysts from ever specifying their own range.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Relying purely on analyst discipline to always remember a WHERE clause does not provide a technical safeguard against accidental full scans — the requirement explicitly asks for a mechanism that avoids this risk even if someone forgets, which a view alone (without a scan-limiting control) doesn't provide.

B – Incorrect. Redshift Spectrum does have a real per-TB-scanned cost model very similar to Athena's; claiming it has no cost at all is factually incorrect, and switching engines doesn't address the flexible-parameterization or scan-limiting requirements either.

C – Correct. Athena prepared statements let a single parameterized query template accept arbitrary start/end date inputs, satisfying the flexible multi-month/cross-year range requirement without hand-writing a new query each time, while an Athena workgroup's per-query bytes-scanned control provides an automatic technical guardrail that cancels any query (including one where a filter was omitted) exceeding a defined scan threshold — directly addressing both stated requirements together.

D – Incorrect. Hardcoding the date range server-side directly contradicts the stated requirement that finance be able to specify arbitrary custom date ranges — this removes the flexibility being requested rather than delivering it safely.
topic: Athena prepared statements allow a single query template to be reused with different runtime parameters (like arbitrary date ranges), avoiding the need to hand-author new SQL per request, while Athena workgroup-level data usage controls (a configurable bytes-scanned ceiling per query) provide an automated technical guardrail against runaway or accidentally unfiltered queries — independent of whether individual analysts remember to filter correctly. The exam-pattern trigger combining 'flexible parameterized query needs' with 'must prevent accidental full-table scans' points to this specific pairing of Athena features rather than relying on documentation/training, view definitions alone, or switching query engines.

question: A data engineering team ingests IoT sensor telemetry through an AWS Glue streaming ETL job that reads from Kinesis Data Streams, performs 10-minute tumbling window aggregations, and writes results to S3. Yesterday, the on-call engineer received a CloudWatch Alarm indicating the Glue streaming job had zero output written to S3 for over 40 minutes, but the job's own run status in the Glue console still showed 'Running' rather than 'Failed', and Kinesis Data Streams metrics showed IncomingRecords continuing normally at the expected rate the entire time, meaning data was still arriving in the stream. The engineer needs to distinguish between several plausible causes: the Glue job's Spark micro-batches silently stalling without erroring out, an IteratorAge buildup on the Kinesis shards the job is reading from indicating the consumer has fallen behind, or an issue in the S3 write path itself (such as a permissions or throttling problem causing writes to fail silently). Which single CloudWatch metric would most directly confirm whether the Glue streaming job's Kinesis consumer is actually falling behind versus stalled entirely on the write side?
options: Glue's Filtered Bytes metric, since it shows how much data was excluded by the job's transformation logic during each run.
NumberOfObjects for the destination S3 bucket, since a static object count over the 40-minute window directly proves the Glue job has stopped reading from Kinesis entirely.
PutRecords.Success for the Kinesis stream, since it reflects whether producer writes into the stream are succeeding.
GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds for the Kinesis stream: a climbing value shows the consumer reading progressively older data and falling behind, while a flat/low value points away from read lag.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Filtered Bytes describes how much data a transform excluded during processing, which is unrelated to diagnosing whether the consumer is lagging on reads versus failing on writes.

B – Incorrect. A static S3 object count is consistent with multiple different root causes (a stalled Spark micro-batch OR a Kinesis read lag OR a genuine S3 write failure) — it doesn't by itself distinguish which of those is actually happening, whereas IteratorAge specifically isolates the read-lag hypothesis.

C – Incorrect. PutRecords.Success reflects producer-side write success into the stream, not consumer-side read behavior — the scenario already confirms IncomingRecords is healthy, so producer-side metrics don't help distinguish between the three consumer-side/write-side hypotheses being investigated.

D – Correct. GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds measures how far behind (in time) the consumer's current read position is relative to the latest data in the shard; a climbing IteratorAge conclusively indicates the Glue job's Kinesis consumer is falling behind on reads, whereas a flat/low IteratorAge with continuing IncomingRecords would rule out a read-side lag and point the investigation toward the write path (S3 permissions/throttling) or a stalled Spark micro-batch instead — this metric specifically isolates the read-side hypothesis from the others.
topic: GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds is the definitive Kinesis consumer-lag metric: it measures the time difference between the current time and the timestamp of the last record read, so a climbing value directly proves the consumer is falling behind on reads, while a flat/near-zero value rules out read-side lag as the cause of a stalled pipeline. This is a hard troubleshooting pattern because multiple plausible failure modes (stalled processing, consumer lag, write-path failure) can all present as 'no new output for 40 minutes,' and the exam wants recognition of which specific metric isolates which specific hypothesis rather than a generic 'check CloudWatch' answer.

question: A healthcare data platform spans 3 AWS accounts in an AWS Organization: a central governed-lake account holding the Glue Data Catalog and raw/curated S3 data registered in Lake Formation, a clinical-research account whose data scientists need read access to de-identified patient tables, and a billing-analytics account whose analysts need read access only to claims tables. The security team wants to grant cross-account access to specific databases such that clinical-research can only ever see de-identified patient tables (never the raw PII tables in the same database) and billing-analytics can only ever see claims tables, using a single centralized permission model rather than per-account IAM policies duplicated three times, and wants any future change in row/column-level restrictions applied once and automatically respected by every consuming account's query engine (Athena in both accounts). Which architecture satisfies this?
options: Use Lake Formation cross-account grants from the central account to share only the de-identified tables with clinical-research and only the claims tables with billing-analytics.
Create identical copies of the de-identified patient tables and claims tables in each consuming account's own S3 bucket and Glue Data Catalog via a scheduled Glue ETL job.
Grant each consuming account's IAM roles direct s3:GetObject permissions on the entire central S3 bucket, relying on each account's own Athena workgroup configuration to filter accessible prefixes.
Set up VPC peering between all 3 accounts and restrict access to the central data lake based solely on which VPC the query originates from.
explanations: A – Correct. Lake Formation supports cross-account data sharing through resource links and grants, where fine-grained (table/column/row-level) permissions are defined centrally once in the account that owns the data and are automatically enforced for consuming accounts' query engines — this exactly matches the requirement for a single centralized model, precise per-account visibility (de-identified only vs. claims only), and automatic propagation of future permission changes without duplicating IAM policy logic three times.

B – Incorrect. Duplicating data via scheduled ETL creates copies that can drift out of sync with the source, doubles storage cost, and means any future change to row/column restrictions must be manually re-applied to every copy separately — the opposite of 'applied once and automatically respected everywhere.'

C – Incorrect. Direct bucket-level IAM permissions bypass Lake Formation's fine-grained table/column/row filtering entirely — granting s3:GetObject on the whole bucket would expose the raw PII tables to clinical-research along with the de-identified ones, violating the requirement that PII tables must never be visible to that account; Athena workgroup configuration doesn't provide row/column-level data governance either.

D – Incorrect. VPC peering controls network-layer connectivity, not data-layer authorization — it has no mechanism for restricting which specific tables, columns, or rows a query can return, so it cannot satisfy the fine-grained, per-account visibility requirement described.
topic: Lake Formation cross-account sharing (via resource links granted from a central data-lake account to consuming accounts) provides one centralized place to define table, column, and row-level permissions that are then automatically enforced by any Lake Formation-integrated query engine (Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR) in every consuming account — permissions don't need to be re-defined per account. The exam-pattern trigger is 'centralized data lake, multiple consuming accounts need different fine-grained visibility into the same underlying tables, want a single point of control' — this is squarely Lake Formation's cross-account grant model, as distinguished from copying data (creates drift/duplication) or relying on IAM/network-layer controls alone (neither can express column/row-level restrictions).

question: A multinational retailer's central data platform account holds a customer_transactions table in S3, encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key (arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:111111111111:key/central-key) owned by the platform account (111111111111). A newly onboarded regional analytics account (222222222222) needs read access for its Athena users to query this table, and Lake Formation has already been used to grant that account's IAM role SELECT permission on the table via a cross-account grant. After setting this up, users in the regional account can see the table listed and can successfully run Athena queries that return column names and structure, but every query fails at execution time with an access denied error referencing the KMS key when actually reading the underlying encrypted S3 objects. What is missing?
options: Lake Formation cross-account grants only support unencrypted S3 data; the table must be re-encrypted using SSE-S3 instead of a customer-managed KMS key before sharing will work.
The central account's KMS key policy must explicitly grant the regional account's Athena/Glue role kms:Decrypt, since Lake Formation and S3 grants alone don't cover decrypting another account's key.
The regional account needs its own separate customer-managed KMS key associated with the Lake Formation grant, since a KMS key's key policy cannot list principals from another AWS account.
The regional account's Athena workgroup needs s3:GetObject added to its IAM policy, since Lake Formation's service-linked access covers table metadata but not the underlying object bytes.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Lake Formation cross-account sharing works with KMS-encrypted data; there's no such restriction — this is a fabricated limitation, and re-encrypting with SSE-S3 (which uses AWS-managed keys with no customer control over cross-account key policies in this scenario's context) isn't the correct or expected fix and would need to be revisited if fine-grained key control were later required.

B – Correct. This is the classic cross-account KMS gotcha: even with correct Lake Formation permissions and S3-level access granted, a customer-managed KMS key's key policy is a separate, independent layer of access control — the key owner (the central platform account) must explicitly add the regional account's relevant principal (its Athena/Glue execution role) to the KMS key policy with kms:Decrypt permission, or reads of the encrypted objects will fail even though every other layer of access looks correctly configured.

C – Incorrect. KMS key policies can absolutely list principals from another AWS account, granting them permission to use the key — that is the standard supported cross-account mechanism (as described in option B); creating a duplicate key in the regional account would not decrypt data encrypted under the central account's key, since decryption requires the actual key that encrypted the data.

D – Incorrect. Lake Formation's fine-grained permissions model handles the underlying S3 data access on the consuming principal's behalf via its own service-linked mechanisms once granted — the failure described (specifically referencing the KMS key at execution time, after successfully listing/describing the table) points to the well-documented KMS cross-account decrypt gap, not a missing raw S3 IAM action.
topic: Cross-account access to KMS-encrypted S3 data requires two independent, additive layers of permission: resource-level access (an S3 bucket policy or, here, a Lake Formation grant) AND an explicit grant on the KMS key policy itself allowing the other account's principal to use that specific key for kms:Decrypt — missing either layer causes access to fail, often confusingly late (only at actual object-read time, after metadata/listing operations already succeeded). This is one of the most heavily tested hard-tier patterns on the exam specifically because every other layer (Lake Formation, IAM, S3) can look fully correct while the KMS key policy is the actual, less-obvious gap.

question: A financial services company must satisfy an auditor's request to determine exactly which IAM principal ran a specific Athena query against a restricted customer_pii table on March 3rd, what SQL text was executed, and whether that principal's access was granted via a Lake Formation row-filter that limited results to only a subset of records. The company's default CloudTrail trail currently only captures management events, and the compliance team also needs to be able to run ad-hoc SQL queries against 2 years of this audit history going forward for periodic reviews, rather than paging through the CloudTrail console's default 90-day event history view. What combination of configuration changes is required?
options: Enable CloudWatch Logs Insights on the Athena service logs, since Insights natively retains 2 years of query history and supports SQL-style querying without any CloudTrail configuration changes.
Rely on Lake Formation's own built-in audit dashboard, which independently retains 2 years of query-level history with SQL text by default with no additional configuration required.
Enable AWS Config rules on the Athena workgroup to track every query executed as a configuration item, then query AWS Config's configuration history for the March 3rd date range.
Configure a CloudTrail trail (or CloudTrail Lake) to capture Athena/Lake Formation data events plus management events with 2-year retention, then use CloudTrail Lake's SQL query capability.
explanations: A – Incorrect. CloudWatch Logs Insights queries existing CloudWatch Logs data with whatever retention has been configured on the log group — it does not natively retain 2 years by default, and critically, Athena query auditing (who ran what, from where) is a CloudTrail data event concern, not something automatically captured in CloudWatch Logs without corresponding trail configuration.

B – Incorrect. Lake Formation does not provide its own independent, separately-retained 2-year query audit dashboard with this level of detail by default; query-level audit trail for Athena is sourced from CloudTrail, not a built-in Lake Formation feature — this option describes a capability that doesn't exist as stated.

C – Incorrect. AWS Config tracks resource configuration state and drift over time (e.g., whether a security group's rules changed), not individual query executions or API call events — it is not designed to and does not capture 'who ran this specific SQL query' information.

D – Correct. By default, CloudTrail's console Event History only shows the last 90 days of management events, and detailed per-query data events (like Athena StartQueryExecution calls) are not captured unless a trail or CloudTrail Lake event data store is explicitly configured to include data events. Configuring this with an appropriate retention window (up to and including 2+ years in CloudTrail Lake) and using CloudTrail Lake's native SQL query capability against the event data satisfies both the specific March 3rd investigation and the ongoing ad-hoc 2-year audit query requirement in one coherent solution.
topic: CloudTrail's Event History console view only retains the last 90 days of management events by default, and fine-grained data events (individual API calls like Athena query executions or S3 object-level access) require explicitly configuring a trail or CloudTrail Lake event data store to capture them — they are not captured automatically. CloudTrail Lake specifically supports running SQL queries directly against retained event data with configurable long-term retention, making it the right answer whenever a scenario needs both historical (multi-year) audit investigation and ongoing ad-hoc SQL-based audit querying, as opposed to AWS Config (tracks configuration state/drift, not individual API calls) or assuming any service retains detailed audit history indefinitely by default.

question: A pharmaceutical company's data science team wants to build a Retrieval-Augmented Generation application using an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base backed by a vector index over internal clinical trial documents stored in S3. The documents span two research divisions in two separate AWS accounts under the same AWS Organization: Division A's account owns oncology trial documents, and Division B's account owns cardiology trial documents. Corporate policy strictly prohibits any cross-division access to raw source documents (an oncology researcher must never be able to read a cardiology document or vice versa), but leadership wants a single unified Bedrock knowledge base and chat interface that both divisions' researchers can query, where each researcher's questions are answered only using their own division's documents, never the other division's. Which architecture satisfies the strict data-isolation requirement while still supporting a single interface?
options: Build one shared Bedrock knowledge base and vector index, and rely solely on IAM resource policies on the knowledge base to filter which document chunks are returned per researcher at query time.
Build two separate knowledge bases, one per division, each scoped to that division's own account/IAM boundary, fronted by one orchestration layer routing queries by identity.
Merge both divisions' S3 buckets into one central account's bucket, then use S3 Object Lock in governance mode to prevent cross-division reads after ingestion.

Build one Bedrock knowledge base with a single shared vector index ingesting both divisions' documents, relying on prompt engineering to tell the model to only reference the querying researcher's division.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Bedrock knowledge base vector retrieval does not provide fine-grained IAM-resource-policy-based filtering of individual document chunks within a shared index at the level of strict per-division data segregation — mixing both divisions' documents into one index creates the same fundamental risk as option A, just described as an IAM control that doesn't actually operate at that granularity for vector retrieval content.

B – Correct. Maintaining two genuinely separate knowledge bases, each ingesting only its own division's source documents and scoped within that division's own account/IAM boundary, ensures Division B's raw documents are never even present in an index reachable by Division A's queries or vice versa — a real access-control boundary rather than a soft instruction. A single orchestration/routing layer on top (directing each authenticated researcher's query to the correct knowledge base) preserves the single unified interface experience without weakening the underlying isolation.

C – Incorrect. Physically merging the source documents into one bucket, even with Object Lock (which prevents deletion/overwrite, not access control), does nothing to prevent a Division A principal from reading a Division B document — Object Lock is a retention/immutability control, not an access-isolation control, and this approach directly violates the 'must never read the other division's documents' requirement by co-locating them without effective access separation.

D – Incorrect. Prompt engineering instructions are not a security or access-control boundary — a model instructed to 'only use Division A documents' can still be manipulated (via prompt injection or model error) into surfacing content from Division B's documents that are physically present in the same shared vector index; this doesn't satisfy a strict prohibition on cross-division access.
topic: When strict data isolation between groups is required even while supporting a shared user-facing interface, the pattern is separate underlying resources (here, separate Bedrock knowledge bases/vector indexes, each scoped to its own account/IAM boundary) fronted by a single routing/orchestration layer — not a single shared resource relying on prompt instructions, in-application filtering, or non-access-control mechanisms (like Object Lock) to enforce the boundary. This is a newer 2025/2026-scope Bedrock knowledge base governance pattern the exam tests by analogy to older multi-tenant isolation scenarios: the underlying principle (real access boundary vs. soft/logical separation) is identical to classic Lake Formation/IAM isolation questions, just applied to a vector index.

question: A retail analytics company runs Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio for its combined data engineering and data science organization. The governance team has set up a domain with several domain units mapping to business functions: 'Marketing Analytics,' 'Supply Chain,' and 'Finance.' Within Marketing Analytics, two active projects exist: 'Campaign Attribution' and 'Customer Segmentation.' A data scientist named Priya is a member of the Campaign Attribution project only. She reports that she can browse and discover a curated customer_ltv dataset that is registered as a governed asset under the Customer Segmentation project, including seeing its name, description, and schema in the catalog, but she is unable to actually query or export its underlying data. Is this the expected behavior, and why?
options: No — this is a misconfiguration. Domain units are purely organizational folders with no access-control function; Priya's inability to query the data must be an unrelated IAM gap that should be fixed so she gets full access.
Yes — expected. Discoverability (name/schema) and data access (query/export) are governed separately; finding an asset doesn't grant permission to use its data.

Yes, but only because Priya's IAM role lacks s3:GetObject on the underlying bucket; adding that one permission would make discoverability and access functionally identical for all governed assets going forward.

No — this is a misconfiguration. Once a governed asset is published to any project within a domain unit, all members of every project in that domain unit automatically receive full query/export access.
explanations: A – Incorrect. This mischaracterizes SageMaker Catalog's governance model — discoverability and usability are intentionally separate layers, so Priya's experience is not automatically evidence of a misconfigured IAM gap; it's the designed behavior of the governed-sharing model.

B – Correct. SageMaker Catalog (and the broader SageMaker Unified Studio governance model) is explicitly designed so that governed data assets can be made discoverable across a domain (so users can find out what data exists, understand its schema/description, and request access) without that discoverability automatically granting the ability to actually query or export the underlying data — genuine data access still requires project membership for the owning project or an explicit separate grant to that specific asset. This two-tier model (discover vs. use) is exactly what the scenario describes, and it is the intended, expected behavior.

C – Incorrect. This oversimplifies the governance model to a single IAM permission; SageMaker Catalog's asset-level access grants are the actual governing mechanism for data usage, and simply adding a raw S3 permission bypassing the catalog's own access model would undermine the governed-sharing design rather than correctly resolve it.

D – Incorrect. Project membership does not automatically cascade access across sibling projects within the same domain unit — 'Campaign Attribution' and 'Customer Segmentation' are separate projects with independently governed asset access, even though they sit under the same 'Marketing Analytics' domain unit.
topic: SageMaker Unified Studio / SageMaker Catalog implements a deliberate two-tier governance model: domains and domain units organize projects, and governed assets can be published for org-wide discoverability (browsing name/schema/description) independent from actual data usage rights, which still require project membership or an explicit per-asset access grant. The exam-pattern trigger for this newer-scope topic is a user who can 'see' or 'find' a governed asset but cannot use its data — that's the intended discover-vs-access separation working correctly, not a bug, and recognizing this two-tier model (rather than assuming visibility implies access, or that project-adjacency implies access) is the specific skill being tested.

question: A logistics company's security team is investigating a potential data exfiltration incident: a large volume of objects were downloaded from a sensitive S3 bucket over a weekend using valid IAM credentials belonging to a departed contractor whose access should have been revoked the previous Friday. The team needs to determine, across the prior 18 months, every single S3 GetObject call made by that contractor's IAM user, including timestamps and source IP addresses, to build a complete picture for a potential legal proceeding. The company's S3 buckets currently have only the default account-level CloudTrail trail enabled, which the security team already suspects will be insufficient. What must have already been in place, and what should be configured going forward to prevent this gap for future investigations?
options: The default trail captures only management events, not data events like GetObject; data event logging had to be enabled in advance, and past calls can't be recovered now.

Nothing additional was needed; the default CloudTrail trail captures all S3 GetObject calls automatically for all buckets going back at least 18 months, so the historical data should already be fully available.
S3 Server Access Logging alone would have automatically captured everything CloudTrail data events would have, making CloudTrail data event configuration unnecessary going forward.
AWS Config should be configured now and pointed at its configuration-item history to reconstruct the 18-month record of GetObject calls, since Config change history covers object-level S3 access.
explanations: A – Correct. S3 object-level API activity (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) are CloudTrail data events, which are not captured by the default trail and must be explicitly enabled on a trail (or configured in a CloudTrail Lake event data store) in advance of when the activity occurs. Since this wasn't configured, the granular historical GetObject record likely doesn't exist and can't be retroactively reconstructed — the security team should configure this going forward to close the gap for future incidents, while acknowledging the current investigation may be limited to whatever other signals are available (like S3 Server Access Logs, if those happened to be enabled).

B – Incorrect. This is factually wrong and is exactly the gap the security team suspects — the default CloudTrail trail captures management events (like CreateBucket, PutBucketPolicy) but does NOT capture data events (like individual GetObject/PutObject calls) unless a trail is explicitly configured to include them; without that prior configuration, this granular history was never being recorded at all.

C – Incorrect. S3 Server Access Logging is a separate, S3-specific logging mechanism (delivered as log files to another S3 bucket) that is also not enabled by default and must be turned on in advance — its existence doesn't retroactively fill a CloudTrail data event gap, and the scenario doesn't establish it was enabled either; it's also not automatically equivalent to or a substitute for CloudTrail data events in terms of format or integration with other CloudTrail-based tooling.

D – Incorrect. AWS Config tracks resource configuration state over time, not individual object-level API access events — it has no mechanism to reconstruct historical GetObject call history, retroactively or otherwise; this conflates Config's configuration-drift tracking with CloudTrail's API-activity logging.
topic: CloudTrail's default trail captures only management events; capturing S3 object-level data events (GetObject, PutObject, DeleteObject) requires explicitly configuring a trail (or CloudTrail Lake event data store) to include data events, and this must be done proactively — there is no way to retroactively generate historical data-event records for a period before that configuration existed. This is a hard, consequence-heavy exam pattern: recognizing that the default trail is insufficient for granular object-access forensics, and that the gap for past events is permanent and unrecoverable, distinguishes real understanding from the common (and here incorrect) assumption that 'CloudTrail logs everything by default.'

question: A biotech company operating under GDPR must ensure that all data belonging to EU research subjects is stored and processed exclusively within EU AWS Regions, and that this restriction is enforced organization-wide as a hard technical control rather than relying on individual engineering teams to remember Region selection correctly. The company has 40 AWS accounts under a single AWS Organization, all currently able to create resources in any AWS Region. The compliance team also requires that even an engineer with full administrative IAM permissions within an individual account must be structurally prevented from spinning up a non-compliant resource (such as an RDS instance in us-east-1 containing EU subject data) — a written policy or code-review process alone is explicitly deemed insufficient. What should the company implement?
options: Apply a Service Control Policy (SCP) at the Organizations level that denies resource-creation API calls outside the approved EU Regions, attached to the relevant OUs so it overrides even an individual IAM administrator's own permissions.
Publish an internal engineering wiki page and a mandatory annual training module documenting approved Regions, and require engineers to self-attest compliance during code review.
Configure AWS Config rules in each account to flag non-EU-Region resources after they are created, and rely on the compliance team manually reviewing and remediating flagged findings weekly.

Grant only a single centralized Region Approver IAM role permission to launch resources in any Region, and have all 40 accounts' engineers request temporary elevated access through that role for every deployment.
explanations: A – Correct. Service Control Policies (SCPs) applied at the AWS Organizations level are the described preventative, account-wide technical control: an SCP denying resource creation outside approved Regions overrides even an account's own IAM administrator permissions, because SCPs set the maximum permission boundary for every principal in the account — no IAM policy, however permissive, can grant access to an action an SCP explicitly denies. This structurally prevents non-compliant resource creation rather than just detecting it after the fact, matching every stated requirement.

B – Incorrect. Written policy and training are explicitly the kind of non-technical control the compliance team has ruled insufficient — they rely on individuals remembering and complying, which is exactly the gap the requirement demands be closed with a hard technical control.

C – Incorrect. AWS Config with manual weekly remediation is a detective control, not a preventative one — it identifies non-compliant resources after they've already been created (and potentially already processed EU subject data in a non-compliant Region), which doesn't satisfy the requirement for the restriction to be structurally prevented in the first place.

D – Incorrect. Manually gating all deployments through a single centralized role across 40 accounts for every deployment is an operationally unscalable process-based workaround, not a systematic technical guardrail, and doesn't actually prevent an administrator within an account from bypassing the process using their own existing permissions unless the account's IAM is itself restricted — which is exactly what an SCP does more directly and reliably.
topic: Service Control Policies (SCPs) applied at the AWS Organizations level are the strongest preventative technical control for enforcing data sovereignty/Region restrictions: because SCPs define the maximum available permissions for every principal in an account (including administrators), a Region-restricting SCP structurally prevents resource creation in disallowed Regions organization-wide, regardless of any individual account's own IAM configuration. The exam-pattern trigger is 'must be a hard/structural/technical control, not reliant on individual compliance, applies even to admins, organization-wide' — that combination specifically points to SCPs rather than detective controls (Config), documentation/training, or account-level IAM policies that individual admins could still override within their own account.

question: A company's compliance team discovers, via an Amazon Macie scan of its S3 data lake, that a bucket believed to contain only anonymized marketing analytics data actually contains several thousand objects with unredacted customer Social Security numbers and full names, apparently introduced by an upstream data source that stopped anonymizing records six months ago without anyone noticing. The bucket is registered in Lake Formation and queried by both an internal analytics team (via Athena) and an external marketing agency (via a cross-account Lake Formation grant). The compliance team needs to immediately stop the external agency's continued exposure to this PII while the internal team investigates and remediates the root cause, without disrupting the internal analytics team's ongoing legitimate access to the (mostly clean) rest of the dataset. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Revoke all IAM permissions for both the internal analytics team and the external marketing agency simultaneously, fully shutting down all access to the bucket, including the internal team's unrelated legitimate work, until the root cause is resolved.
Delete the entire S3 bucket immediately to eliminate all exposure risk, then rebuild the dataset from scratch once the anonymization pipeline is fixed.

Revoke or narrow the cross-account Lake Formation grant to the marketing agency (e.g., removing access to the affected table, or restricting via a row/column filter), leaving the internal team's Lake Formation permissions unchanged pending remediation.

Do nothing at the access-control layer since Macie only produces findings and has no integration with actual data access enforcement; wait for the upstream source to fix anonymization before taking any action.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Cutting off the internal analytics team's access entirely is overly broad and unnecessary — the scenario specifically asks for a response that stops external exposure while preserving the internal team's legitimate access to the rest of the (mostly clean) dataset; this option fails that explicit constraint.

B – Incorrect. Deleting the entire bucket is a drastic, disproportionate action that destroys legitimate clean data alongside the compromised subset, disrupts the internal team's ongoing work entirely, and doesn't represent a targeted, appropriately-scoped incident response.

C – Correct. Macie identifies risk (unexpected PII); the actual enforcement of restricted access is Lake Formation and IAM's job — this is the documented two-step governance workflow the exam emphasizes. Since the specific concern is external exposure of newly-discovered PII, targeted narrowing/revocation of the external agency's cross-account grant (or restricting via row/column filtering to exclude compromised records) directly and immediately addresses that exposure without collaterally disrupting the internal team's legitimate, ongoing access to the broader dataset.

D – Incorrect. This mischaracterizes the intended Macie-to-Lake-Formation workflow — Macie findings are explicitly meant to feed into and trigger tightening of Lake Formation/IAM access controls as the next step; treating a live PII exposure finding as something to simply wait out is not an appropriate incident response and ignores the documented governance pattern of the two tools working together.
topic: Amazon Macie identifies and surfaces sensitive-data risk (unexpected PII in S3) but does not itself enforce or restrict access — that enforcement responsibility sits with Lake Formation (fine-grained table/column/row permissions) and IAM, forming a documented two-step pipeline: Macie discovers, Lake Formation/IAM restrict. The exam-pattern trigger is a Macie finding followed by a question about the appropriate next action — the correct move is always a targeted tightening of Lake Formation/IAM permissions scoped to the actual exposure (here, the external cross-account grant), not disproportionate actions like full deletion or blanket access revocation, and not treating Macie as if it can block access on its own.

question: A company's platform team allows individual data engineers across several teams to self-service create their own IAM roles for the Glue jobs they build, since centralizing every role creation through the platform team was creating a bottleneck. However, the security team must guarantee that no engineer can ever create (or modify an existing role into) a role with iam:PassRole combined with wildcard resource access, or with permissions broader than what's needed for standard Glue/S3/Redshift operations, since either combination could be used to escalate privileges. The security team wants this enforced automatically at the moment of role creation or modification, not detected after the fact via a periodic scan. What should they implement?
options: Attach a permissions boundary to every self-service-created role, capping its maximum permissions regardless of the engineer's own permissions, enforced at creation/modification time.
Rely on IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation warnings alone, since Access Analyzer automatically blocks any IAM API call that would create an over-permissioned role.
Require engineers to submit a support ticket for every individual role creation, reintroducing the exact centralized bottleneck the platform team was trying to eliminate.
Configure an AWS Config rule that evaluates all IAM roles daily and flags any role matching the prohibited permission patterns for manual remediation.
explanations: A – Correct. A permissions boundary is an IAM feature specifically designed for this delegated-role-creation scenario: it sets the maximum permissions a role can have regardless of what policy is directly attached to it, enforced natively and immediately by IAM at the API call level (role creation/modification), not via a subsequent scan. Requiring the boundary on all self-service-created roles means engineers retain the ability to create their own roles (preserving the self-service model) while being structurally incapable of granting permissions beyond the boundary's ceiling — directly satisfying real-time, preventative enforcement of the prohibited permission combinations.

B – Incorrect. IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation provides warnings and recommendations during policy authoring in supported workflows, but it does not itself function as an enforcement mechanism that blocks IAM API calls outright — this mischaracterizes Access Analyzer's actual capability; permissions boundaries are the correct native IAM enforcement mechanism for capping delegated role creation.

C – Incorrect. This reintroduces exactly the centralized-bottleneck problem the platform team was trying to solve by allowing self-service role creation in the first place — it doesn't represent a scalable technical control.

D – Incorrect. AWS Config evaluating roles daily is explicitly a detective, after-the-fact control — the security team's stated requirement is enforcement 'at the moment of role creation or modification, not detected after the fact,' which a daily Config scan does not satisfy since a role could exist and even be used before the next evaluation cycle catches it.
topic: IAM permissions boundaries set the maximum permissions an IAM role or user can ever have, enforced natively by IAM at the moment any policy is evaluated — including at role creation/modification time — regardless of what the creating principal's own permissions would otherwise allow. This is the standard pattern for safely delegating self-service IAM role creation: attach a boundary policy that excludes dangerous combinations (like unrestricted iam:PassRole) to every role engineers are permitted to create, preserving decentralized self-service while structurally preventing privilege escalation, as distinct from detective controls (AWS Config, Access Analyzer warnings) that only catch problems after the fact.

question: A global manufacturing company runs Amazon Redshift as its central data warehouse, storing production data from factories in Germany, Japan, and the United States all in shared fact tables. German factory data is subject to GDPR and must never be visible to Redshift users outside the EU data governance team, and separately, factory-floor engineers in each country should only see operational data for their own country's factories regardless of role. The company wants both restrictions enforced with a single mechanism that scales as new countries and factories are added over time, without needing to write and maintain a separate Redshift view or GRANT statement combination for every new country/role pairing that gets introduced. Which authorization approach best fits?
options: A single shared Redshift role granted to all users with SELECT on all fact tables, relying entirely on BI-tool-layer filtering to hide rows from users based on their country.
RBAC: a dedicated Redshift database role for every country, users assigned to the role matching their country, with views manually filtered per role.

ABAC, where access decisions are computed at query time from attributes like the user's country/team compared against the row's country/classification attributes, instead of a growing list of per-country roles and views.
Tag-based access control applied only at the S3 storage layer beneath Redshift, since Redshift itself has no concept of row-level filtering and all filtering must happen before data reaches Redshift.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Relying entirely on BI-tool-layer filtering while granting full underlying SELECT access at the database layer means any user who queries Redshift directly (bypassing the BI tool) would see all countries' data unfiltered, including the GDPR-restricted German data — this fails to provide actual data-layer enforcement and is a serious security gap.

B – Incorrect. RBAC with a dedicated role per country works today but is explicitly what the requirement wants to avoid at scale — 'without needing to write and maintain a separate view or GRANT combination for every new country/role pairing' directly describes RBAC's known weakness: it becomes unwieldy as the number of distinct roles/combinations grows, requiring new roles and views to be created and maintained for every new country added.

C – Correct. ABAC computes access decisions dynamically at request/query time from attributes on both the principal (the user's assigned country, team, GDPR-clearance status) and the resource (the row's country/classification), rather than requiring a static, manually maintained list of permitted role/resource combinations — this is exactly suited to a scenario emphasizing scale and frequent addition of new countries/factories, since new attribute values (a new country) are handled by the same general policy logic without creating new roles or views each time.

D – Incorrect. Redshift does support row-level security (via views or native row-level security features) — this option incorrectly claims Redshift has no row-filtering concept, and pushing all filtering to the S3 layer beneath Redshift doesn't address that Redshift itself needs to enforce access on structured query results.
topic: Attribute-based access control (ABAC) computes access decisions dynamically from attributes on both the principal and the resource at request time, rather than requiring a growing, statically maintained set of roles or resource-specific grants — making it the best fit whenever a scenario explicitly emphasizes scale and frequent growth in the number of distinct groups/resources needing differentiated access (here, new countries/factories added over time). The exam consistently favors ABAC as the answer for this 'scales better as things grow' pattern, distinguishing it from RBAC (simple but grows unwieldy with many roles) and tag-based access control (resource-tag-driven, a narrower special case of the same general idea).

question: A company's data lake stores customer support call transcripts in S3, which are indexed into an Amazon Kendra index for enterprise search used by customer support agents, account managers, and the legal team. Some transcripts contain privileged attorney-client communications that only the legal team should be able to find and read via search; all other transcripts should be searchable by all three groups. The company already uses Lake Formation to govern structured tables elsewhere in its data lake, but Kendra indexes unstructured documents directly from S3, not through Lake Formation-governed tables. What is the correct way to ensure only the legal team's search results include the privileged transcripts, while all groups still see the non-privileged transcripts in a single shared Kendra index?
options: Configure Kendra document-level access control using each transcript's ACL or user/group attribute metadata, so at query time Kendra filters results per user against each document's configured permissions.

Register the S3 bucket containing the transcripts as a Lake Formation-governed resource, since Lake Formation permissions automatically apply to any Kendra index built on top of an S3 location once registered.

Rely on IAM policies attached to each user restricting which S3 prefixes they can read directly, since Kendra automatically inherits and enforces the querying user's underlying S3 IAM permissions for every document.
Create two entirely separate Kendra indexes, one containing only privileged transcripts accessible solely to legal, and mirror every non-privileged transcript into both indexes.
explanations: A – Correct. Amazon Kendra supports document-level access control, where each document ingested into the index can carry access control list / user-group attribute metadata, and Kendra enforces this at query time by filtering which documents a given querying user is permitted to see in their search results — this allows a single shared index to serve differentiated visibility to different groups without duplicating documents or indexes, directly matching the requirement.

B – Incorrect. Lake Formation governs structured data access for query engines like Athena, Redshift Spectrum, and EMR against catalog-registered tables; it does not extend its permission model to Kendra's unstructured document search/indexing — Kendra document-level ACLs are Kendra's own separate access-control mechanism for this purpose.

C – Incorrect. Kendra does not automatically inherit or enforce a querying user's raw S3 IAM permissions per-document at search time in this way — access control within Kendra search results requires Kendra's own document-level ACL/attribute configuration; underlying S3 IAM permissions alone do not filter Kendra query results per user.

D – Incorrect. This achieves the functional outcome but through unnecessary duplication and operational overhead (maintaining document mirroring/sync across two indexes) when Kendra's native document-level access control accomplishes the same goal within a single index — violates the 'single shared index' preference implied by wanting one consistent search experience without a maintenance burden.
topic: Amazon Kendra (a newer 2025/2026-scope enterprise search service) supports document-level access control via ACLs or attribute-based permissions attached to each ingested document, enforced by Kendra itself at query time to filter results per requesting user — a mechanism distinct from and not inherited from Lake Formation (which governs structured catalog tables) or raw S3 IAM permissions (which Kendra doesn't automatically apply to search-result filtering). The exam-pattern trigger is 'differentiated visibility of unstructured documents within a single shared search index' — recognizing Kendra's own document-level ACL feature, rather than assuming Lake Formation's governance model extends everywhere or that IAM alone handles it, is the specific skill being tested.

question: A pharmaceutical research company must retain detailed audit logs of all data access to its clinical trial data lake for 7 years to satisfy FDA regulatory requirements, including both AWS management-plane events (who changed bucket policies, who modified Lake Formation permissions) and data-plane events (every individual S3 GetObject call against trial data). Separately, the security team wants to be alerted in near-real-time whenever a Lake Formation permission is granted or revoked, since unauthorized permission changes are considered a high-severity security event requiring immediate investigation, not something that should wait for a periodic audit review. Which combination of configurations satisfies both the long-term audit requirement and the near-real-time alerting requirement?
options: Enable S3 Server Access Logging with a 7-year lifecycle policy as the sole audit mechanism, since it captures both management-plane and data-plane events with equivalent detail to CloudTrail.
Configure a CloudTrail trail capturing management and S3 data events with 7-year retention, plus an EventBridge rule on Lake Formation Grant/RevokePermissions events triggering an SNS alert.
Rely solely on AWS Config's configuration history, which natively retains 7 years of history by default and can be configured to send SNS notifications the moment a Lake Formation permission changes.

Configure a single CloudTrail trail capturing both management and data events, delivering logs only to CloudWatch Logs with a 7-year retention policy, and manually review the logs weekly for any Lake Formation permission changes.
explanations: A – Incorrect. S3 Server Access Logging captures S3 request-level activity for that specific bucket but does not capture management-plane events like Lake Formation permission grants/revokes at all — it's not a substitute for CloudTrail's broader event coverage and doesn't satisfy the requirement to audit non-S3 management actions like Lake Formation grants.

B – Correct. This satisfies both requirements distinctly: capturing both management and data events with 7-year retention (via S3 lifecycle or CloudTrail Lake) provides the durable long-term audit trail the FDA requirement demands, while a separate EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail-sourced Lake Formation permission-change API calls, triggering immediate SNS notification, satisfies the near-real-time security alerting requirement — recognizing that CloudTrail events can simultaneously feed both a long-term durable log AND real-time event-driven alerting via EventBridge is the key insight.

C – Incorrect. AWS Config tracks resource configuration state/drift, not individual API call events like GetObject or GrantPermissions calls, and doesn't provide the granular data-plane audit trail (individual object access) required by the FDA-style retention requirement — this conflates Config's capabilities with CloudTrail's.

D – Incorrect. CloudWatch Logs is not the ideal durable, cost-effective long-term retention destination for 7 years of high-volume data events compared to S3 with lifecycle policies or CloudTrail Lake, and weekly manual review directly contradicts the explicit requirement for near-real-time alerting on permission changes.
topic: CloudTrail events can serve two distinct purposes simultaneously: durable delivery to S3 (or CloudTrail Lake) with long-term retention for compliance-driven audit requirements, and real-time event-driven alerting by having EventBridge match on specific CloudTrail-sourced API calls (like Lake Formation's GrantPermissions/RevokePermissions) to trigger immediate notifications via SNS. The exam-pattern trigger is a scenario combining a long-retention audit requirement with a separate near-real-time security alerting requirement on a specific sensitive action — recognizing that one underlying CloudTrail event stream can feed both use cases through different downstream configurations is the key distinction from AWS Config (wrong tool for API-call-level events) or S3 Server Access Logging (doesn't cover non-S3 management events).

question: A company operates a shared Redshift data warehouse used by 5 business units, each of which must be able to query only their own unit's data, with no unit able to see another's rows even within otherwise-shared fact tables, and this restriction must hold even for users connecting directly via SQL client tools with valid database credentials, not just through a BI layer. Separately, the security team wants any new business unit onboarded in the future to require only a configuration change (not new views, new tables, or new GRANT statements written from scratch) to have the same automatic per-unit row isolation applied. The company has already tagged every row with a business_unit_id column. What Redshift feature should they use?
options: Create a separate materialized view per business unit, each pre-filtered to that unit's business_unit_id, and grant each unit's users SELECT only on their view, refreshed on a schedule.
Redshift row-level security (RLS) filters rows via session context (e.g., business_unit_id) at query time, at the engine level, regardless of connection method.
Use Redshift Spectrum external tables with a separate S3 prefix per business unit, migrating away from native Redshift tables entirely to gain per-unit isolation.
Split the shared fact tables into 5 entirely separate physical tables, one per business unit, and grant each business unit's users access only to their own table.
explanations: A – Incorrect. A separate materialized view per unit does achieve row isolation but requires creating (and maintaining refresh schedules for) a new view for every new business unit onboarded — directly violating the stated requirement that onboarding a new unit should require only a configuration change, not new database objects written from scratch.

B – Correct. Redshift row-level security (RLS) policies define filtering logic directly against table rows based on session context/attributes (like the connected user's assigned business_unit_id), and — critically — this enforcement happens at the database engine level, so it applies uniformly regardless of whether the user connects via a BI tool or a raw SQL client with valid credentials, satisfying the 'even for direct SQL client access' requirement. Because the policy is defined generically in terms of a session attribute compared against the business_unit_id column, onboarding a new business unit is a matter of assigning the new session attribute value / role mapping — a configuration change — rather than writing new views, tables, or GRANTs.

C – Incorrect. Migrating from native Redshift tables to Spectrum external tables over S3 is a significant architecture change unrelated to the actual requirement (row-level filtering within existing tables), introduces unnecessary complexity, and doesn't inherently solve the per-unit isolation problem better than RLS does natively within Redshift.

D – Incorrect. Physically splitting into 5 separate tables works for isolation today but means every future new business unit requires creating an entirely new physical table and associated ETL/GRANT logic — the opposite of 'onboarding is a configuration change,' and it also fragments what were previously shared fact tables, complicating any cross-cutting analysis that legitimately needs to span units at a higher governance level.
topic: Redshift row-level security (RLS) policies enforce row filtering directly at the database engine level based on session context (such as a user's assigned attribute/role), meaning the restriction applies universally regardless of connection method — including direct SQL client access, which view-based or BI-tool-layer filtering approaches cannot guarantee. RLS is also designed to scale via configuration (mapping new session attribute values to new roles/groups) rather than requiring new database objects per new segment, directly matching a 'must hold for any connection method' plus 'new groups added later without rebuilding objects' requirement — as opposed to materialized views or physical table-splitting, which both require new objects per new unit.

question: A company's Lake Formation-governed data lake has grown to include 300 tables across 25 databases, accumulated over 4 years with inconsistent tagging and unclear ownership. The governance team wants to migrate from today's ad-hoc, table-by-table permission grants (where individual data engineers manually granted access to specific tables for specific users as requests came in, resulting in an unauditable sprawl of hundreds of individual grants) to a scalable model where access is granted based on a combination of the requesting user's department and clearance-level attributes and each table's data-classification and owning-domain attributes, without needing to enumerate every individual table×user combination that should be permitted, and where a newly added table automatically inherits the correct access rules the moment appropriate classification tags are applied to it. Which Lake Formation capability directly enables this?
options: Lake Formation resource links, which create a pointer from a consuming database to a table in another database, reducing the need for data duplication across databases.
Redshift data sharing, which allows producer clusters to share live data with consumer clusters without duplicating it, avoiding the need for granular Lake Formation table grants entirely.

Lake Formation tag-based access control (LF-TBAC), granting permissions by matching LF-Tags on principals/attributes against tags on databases/tables/columns, instead of a discrete grant per resource.
Lake Formation's default IAMAllowedPrincipals permission model, which grants broad access to any principal with a matching IAM policy, reducing the number of distinct grants needed.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Resource links solve a different problem — making a table registered in one database discoverable/queryable from another database/account context — but they don't change the underlying attribute-based, tag-driven permission-matching model the scenario is asking for; they're still fundamentally about individual resource-level linking, not scalable classification-based grants.

B – Incorrect. Redshift data sharing is a mechanism specific to sharing live data between Redshift clusters/accounts, unrelated to how Lake Formation grants Data Catalog table/column-level permissions to principals across the broader data lake — it doesn't address the described table×user permission sprawl problem.

C – Correct. LF-TBAC lets the governance team define LF-Tags (like classification=confidential, domain=finance) and assign them both to Data Catalog resources (tables/databases/columns) and to principals (or principal attributes), then grant permissions once based on tag-matching logic rather than enumerating every individual table×user grant — this is precisely the attribute-based, tag-driven scaling model described, and newly tagged tables automatically fall under the correct existing tag-based grants without needing new discrete permission entries.

D – Incorrect. IAMAllowedPrincipals is a legacy Lake Formation compatibility setting that effectively defers to underlying IAM policies for access, which is the opposite direction from the fine-grained, centrally governed tag-based model the team wants to move toward — it doesn't provide attribute-based, classification-driven access control at all.
topic: Lake Formation tag-based access control (LF-TBAC) implements attribute-based access control for the data lake: LF-Tags are assigned to both Data Catalog resources (databases, tables, columns) and principals, and permissions are granted by defining rules that match tag combinations rather than enumerating individual resource×principal grants — meaning a newly added or newly tagged table automatically inherits the correct access the moment it receives the relevant tags, with no new discrete grant needed. The exam-pattern trigger is 'permission sprawl from individual resource-level grants, want scale via attributes/classification rather than one-off grants, new resources should automatically inherit correct access' — this maps directly to LF-TBAC as the governance-at-scale answer, distinct from resource links (a different linking mechanism) or the legacy IAMAllowedPrincipals model (the opposite of centralized governance).

question: A company stores customer payment card data in an S3-based data lake, with tokenized card numbers used throughout most downstream analytics pipelines so analysts can join transactions by card without ever seeing real card numbers, but a small fraud-investigation team occasionally needs to recover the actual card number for a specific flagged transaction under documented, audited circumstances (e.g., confirmed fraud escalated to the card network). Separately, customer email addresses are used purely for matching/deduplication across three different upstream source systems that each format emails slightly differently, with no downstream process ever needing to display or recover the original email address itself. Which masking techniques are appropriate for the card numbers and the email addresses, respectively?
options: Hashing for both the card numbers and the email addresses, since hashing is the strongest one-way protection available and should be applied uniformly regardless of downstream use case.
Redaction for both the card numbers and the email addresses, since redaction guarantees neither value can ever be exposed or reconstructed.
Redaction for the card numbers, since payment data is the most sensitive, and tokenization for the email addresses, since they're used for matching across systems.
Tokenization for card numbers, since the fraud team occasionally needs the real value via secure lookup, and hashing for emails, since only one-way matching is needed.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Applying hashing uniformly to the card numbers would make it impossible for the fraud team to ever recover the actual card number, which directly violates their stated occasional legitimate need for the real value — hashing is a poor fit whenever reversibility is required for even a narrow, audited use case.

B – Incorrect. Redaction for both removes the ability to recover the card number for fraud investigation (violating that explicit requirement) and is also unnecessarily destructive for the email use case, where hashing already provides adequate one-way matching capability without needing redaction's complete removal.

C – Incorrect. Redaction removes the value entirely with no way to recover it — this would make it impossible for the fraud team to ever retrieve the actual card number for a legitimately escalated case, directly conflicting with the stated requirement that the real value must occasionally be recoverable under controlled conditions; and tokenization for the emails is unnecessarily reversible when the requirement explicitly states the original email is never needed back.

D – Correct. Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a substitute that can be mapped back to the original via a secure lookup under controlled conditions — exactly matching the fraud team's occasional, audited need to recover the real card number. Hashing applies a one-way transformation ideal for matching/deduplication (identical inputs produce identical hashes, enabling joins across the three source systems) without ever needing or being able to recover the original email — matching the stated 'never needs to display or recover the original value' requirement precisely.
topic: Masking/anonymization technique selection depends entirely on whether the original value is ever needed back downstream: tokenization (reversible via a secure, access-controlled lookup) fits scenarios needing occasional, audited recovery of the real value; hashing (one-way, deterministic for identical inputs) fits scenarios needing only matching/deduplication with no recovery requirement; redaction (irreversible removal) fits scenarios where the value should never be visible or recoverable under any circumstance. The exam-pattern trigger is a scenario stating explicitly whether a value needs to come back later (tokenization), only needs to support joining/matching (hashing), or should never be recoverable at all (redaction) — matching each stated need to its correct technique, rather than defaulting to 'the strongest-sounding' option uniformly, is the specific skill being tested.

question: An insurance company's data platform team is designing IAM for a new AWS Glue ETL pipeline that reads raw policyholder data from an S3 bucket in a shared services account, applies transformations, and writes curated output to a Redshift cluster in the analytics account. The security team's least-privilege review flags the initially proposed IAM policy, which grants the Glue job's execution role s3:* on the entire shared-services bucket (justified by the developer as 'the job might need additional S3 actions as requirements evolve') and redshift:* on the analytics account's cluster (justified as 'simpler to manage one broad statement instead of multiple narrow ones'). The developer argues that AWS-managed policies like AmazonS3FullAccess would be even simpler still. What should the security team require instead, and why?
options: Require a custom policy scoped to the specific S3/Redshift actions the job needs on specific ARNs, rejecting both the wildcard policy and an AWS-managed full-access policy.

Approve the S3 and Redshift wildcard actions as proposed, since IAM policies attached to a role (rather than embedded in application code) already satisfy least privilege regardless of how broad the granted actions are.

Approve the AWS-managed AmazonS3FullAccess policy instead of the custom wildcard policy, since AWS-managed policies are reviewed and maintained by AWS and are therefore inherently more secure than any custom policy a developer could write.

Require the developer to file and re-approve policy exceptions every time the job's requirements change, rather than defining the policy scope now, since anticipating future needs upfront is not possible.
explanations: A – Correct. Least privilege means specifying exact actions (not wildcards like s3:* or redshift:*) and exact resource ARNs (not the entire bucket/cluster) scoped to precisely what the job's actual read/write pattern requires — this is the standard, correct response whenever a proposed policy uses broad wildcards justified by convenience or hypothetical future needs; a custom, narrowly-scoped policy is the textbook expression of least privilege the exam treats as the default correct answer for security tradeoffs like this.

B – Incorrect. Attaching a policy to a role (rather than embedding credentials in code) is a separate, also-important best practice, but it does not by itself satisfy least privilege — the actual permissions granted by that role's policy still matter, and wildcard actions on broad resources violate least privilege regardless of the delegation mechanism.

C – Incorrect. AWS-managed policies are convenient and maintained by AWS, but are deliberately broad to cover many customers' common use cases — this makes them less secure for a specific narrow job, not more secure; the exam explicitly frames managed policies as typically granting more permissions than any single use case actually needs, which is the opposite of least privilege here.

D – Incorrect. While policies can and should evolve over time via proper change management, this option describes an operationally impractical, all-or-nothing extreme (a new approval cycle for every single requirement change) rather than the actual documented answer, which is simply scoping the policy narrowly to current known needs now and iterating through normal change control as requirements genuinely evolve — the correct answer is A's specific scoping guidance, not this process-only deflection.
topic: Least privilege, the exam's default correct answer whenever a security tradeoff scenario is presented, means specifying exact IAM actions (never wildcards like s3:* or service:*) and exact resource ARNs (never *) scoped to precisely what a role's actual operational needs are — and this applies with equal force to AWS-managed policies, which are explicitly broad-by-design to cover many customers' common use cases and therefore typically grant more than any single specific use case needs. The exam-pattern trigger is a developer justifying broad wildcard permissions with 'might need it later' or 'simpler to manage' — the correct response is always a custom, narrowly-scoped policy, rejecting both the wildcard custom policy and the suggestion to fall back on an even broader AWS-managed policy.

question: A company operates a central data lake account (Account H) that owns the Glue Data Catalog and raw S3 data governed by Lake Formation, and 8 business-unit accounts that each consume specific tables via Lake Formation cross-account grants. The security team wants a hub-and-spoke governance model where: (1) all cross-account permission grants must be reviewable and auditable from a single place, (2) if a business-unit account is ever fully offboarded, its access to everything can be revoked with a single action rather than needing to individually revoke dozens of scattered per-table grants, and (3) individual business-unit accounts should never be able to grant sub-access to a fourth account without Account H's explicit approval, even though Lake Formation technically supports grantable permissions that would otherwise allow this. What Lake Formation/organizational configuration achieves all three requirements?
options: Rely on each business-unit account's own CloudTrail logs to reconstruct what access was granted to them, since Lake Formation itself has no centralized way to view all grants issued across accounts.
Grant each business-unit account's IAM administrator direct, unrestricted Lake Formation admin rights within Account H's catalog so they can self-manage their own team's access.
Keep grants issued centrally from Account H (never delegating WITH GRANT OPTION), track each grant by consuming account, and use Account H's listing as the single source of truth.

Have each business-unit account independently configure its own Lake Formation instance mirroring a copy of the relevant tables, eliminating the need for cross-account grants from Account H altogether.
explanations: A – Incorrect. This is factually incorrect — Lake Formation in the central governing account does provide administrative visibility into permissions it has granted; relying on each business-unit account's own separate CloudTrail logs to reconstruct grants is an inferior, fragmented substitute for genuine centralized grant management and doesn't satisfy the single-source-of-truth requirement.

B – Incorrect. Granting business-unit accounts unrestricted Lake Formation admin rights within Account H's catalog directly undermines requirement (1) (single reviewable place) and requirement (3) (preventing sub-delegation without approval) — it decentralizes control in exactly the way the hub-and-spoke model is meant to avoid.

C – Correct. Keeping grant-issuing authority centralized in Account H — specifically never granting 'WITH GRANT OPTION' (grantable permissions) to consuming accounts — directly satisfies requirement (3), since consuming accounts then have no mechanism to sub-delegate access onward without going back through Account H. Issuing and tracking every cross-account grant from Account H against the specific consuming account's principal satisfies requirement (1) (single reviewable/auditable place) and requirement (2) (revoking a single account's central grants cleanly removes its access in one place, since no scattered sub-grants exist to hunt down, because sub-delegation was never permitted in the first place).

D – Incorrect. Independently mirrored per-account Lake Formation instances/data copies reintroduce data duplication, drift risk, and lose the single centralized point of grant management entirely — this contradicts the hub-and-spoke model's core premise and all three stated requirements.
topic: A Lake Formation hub-and-spoke governance model centralizes grant authority in the data-lake-owning account by (a) issuing all cross-account grants from that central account rather than delegating grantable ('WITH GRANT OPTION') permissions to consuming accounts, which prevents uncontrolled sub-delegation, and (b) tracking every grant against the specific consuming account's principal so the central account remains the single source of truth for auditing and can cleanly revoke an entire account's access in one place during offboarding. The exam-pattern trigger is 'centralized data lake account, multiple consuming accounts, must prevent sub-delegation and support single-action full revocation' — this maps to deliberately withholding grantable permissions and keeping all grant issuance centralized, rather than decentralizing admin rights or building parallel independent governance per account.

question: A company runs a data pipeline where an AWS Glue job reads customer records containing dates of birth and Social Security numbers from an encrypted RDS PostgreSQL source, and must write a transformed output to S3 where the SSNs are irreversibly removed for a public-facing aggregate reporting dataset, while a separate internal-only dataset in a different S3 prefix retains a reversible substitute for the SSN so the compliance team can occasionally re-identify a specific record if a customer exercises a GDPR/CCPA data-subject access request. The Glue job's IAM role has full read access to the RDS source and write access to both S3 destination prefixes. A security reviewer flags that both output datasets currently contain the SSN in cleartext, unchanged from the source, despite the stated design intent. What two specific, distinct transformations does the Glue job need to apply to correctly implement the intended design for the two respective output prefixes?
options: Encrypt the SSN column using a customer-managed KMS key for both datasets, and rely on IAM permissions alone (not any data transformation) to differentiate what each audience can see.

Apply hashing to the SSN for both the public-facing dataset and the internal-only dataset, since hashing is deterministic and would allow the compliance team to re-identify records by comparing hash values.

Apply redaction (irreversible removal) to the SSN for the public-facing aggregate dataset, and apply tokenization (a reversible substitute recoverable via a secure lookup) to the SSN for the internal-only dataset used to support data-subject access requests.
