Apply tokenization to the SSN for the public-facing aggregate dataset, and apply redaction to the SSN for the internal-only dataset, since the internal dataset should have the strongest protection since only internal staff access it.
explanations: A – Incorrect. Encryption at rest (via KMS) protects data from unauthorized access at the storage/transport layer but does not itself constitute a masking/anonymization design choice for differentiating what different consumers of the data are meant to see in the value itself — the stated requirement is specifically about which audiences can see/recover the SSN value in the dataset content, which requires an actual masking technique (redaction or tokenization), not encryption-and-IAM alone applied identically to both.

B – Incorrect. Hashing is one-way and does not support recovering the original SSN value; even though identical inputs produce identical hashes (useful for matching/deduplication), the compliance team's stated need is to recover the actual original SSN to respond to a specific data-subject request — hashing cannot provide that, only tokenization's secure-lookup reversibility can.

C – Correct. The public-facing aggregate dataset requires the SSN to be irreversibly removed since it should never be recoverable at all in a broadly-accessible dataset — that's redaction. The internal-only dataset needs the ability to occasionally recover the real SSN under controlled, audited circumstances (to fulfill a specific data-subject access request) — that's tokenization's defining characteristic (a substitute value mappable back to the original via a secure lookup), distinguishing it from both hashing (no recovery) and redaction (no recovery) which are both wrong for this specific internal use case.

D – Incorrect. This reverses the two techniques relative to their actual use cases: the public-facing dataset (which must never expose or allow reconstruction of the SSN under any circumstance) needs redaction, not tokenization's reversibility; the internal dataset (which explicitly needs occasional recovery of the real value) needs tokenization, not redaction, which would make the compliance team's data-subject-request use case impossible to fulfill.
topic: Selecting the correct masking technique depends on whether the original sensitive value must ever be recoverable downstream: redaction is correct when a value must never be visible or reconstructable under any circumstance (a broadly-accessible public/aggregate dataset), while tokenization is correct when a narrow, audited use case (like fulfilling a GDPR/CCPA data-subject access request) requires occasionally recovering the real value via a secure lookup. This is a hard-tier pattern because it requires applying the redaction-vs-tokenization-vs-hashing distinction twice, correctly, to two different destinations within the same pipeline with opposite recoverability requirements — getting either one backwards (as several distractors do) breaks the actual compliance use case.

question: A logistics company's data lake team has been asked by the CISO to implement a control ensuring that any Amazon S3 bucket in the AWS account that stores data classified as 'restricted' can never become publicly accessible, even temporarily, and that this must be enforced automatically and continuously rather than caught only during periodic manual security reviews. Separately, the CISO wants to know, after the fact, precisely which IAM principal changed a specific restricted bucket's policy to (attempt to) make it public last month, even though the attempt was ultimately blocked. The team already has S3 Block Public Access enabled at the account level. Which two additional/complementary controls, mapped correctly to which requirement each one satisfies, should the team implement?
options: Use AWS Config with a managed rule (such as s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited) evaluating continuously with auto-remediation for the 'never public, automatic' requirement, and query CloudTrail for PutBucketPolicy events on the bucket for the 'which principal attempted the change' requirement.

Use only AWS CloudTrail's management events to detect and prevent buckets from ever becoming public, since CloudTrail can be configured to block non-compliant API calls in real time before they take effect.

Use only AWS Config to identify which specific IAM principal attempted to change the bucket policy, since Config configuration items include the full identity of whoever triggered each configuration change.

Rely exclusively on the already-enabled account-level S3 Block Public Access setting for both requirements, since it provides both a continuous preventative control and a full audit trail of every principal who has ever attempted to modify a bucket policy.
explanations: A – Correct. AWS Config continuously evaluates resource configuration state against rules (like the S3 public-read-prohibited managed rule) and, with auto-remediation configured, can automatically correct/flag non-compliant resources on an ongoing basis, satisfying the 'automatically and continuously enforced' requirement — this is a fundamentally different (state-based, continuous) mechanism than Block Public Access (an account-level preventative setting) and adds defense-in-depth. Separately, CloudTrail records the actual API call event (who called PutBucketPolicy, when, from where), which is exactly the tool for determining which specific IAM principal attempted the bucket-policy change last month — matching each tool to the requirement it's actually built for.

B – Incorrect. CloudTrail is a logging/audit service that records API call events after they occur; it does not itself block or prevent API calls from taking effect in real time — that preventative function belongs to policies like Block Public Access or SCPs, not CloudTrail, so this option mischaracterizes CloudTrail's actual capability.

C – Incorrect. While AWS Config configuration items do capture some metadata, determining the specific IAM principal who made a particular API call is CloudTrail's defining purpose (recording who/what/when/source-IP for API calls) — Config is fundamentally about resource configuration state over time, not a substitute for CloudTrail's API-call-level identity attribution.

D – Incorrect. S3 Block Public Access is a valuable preventative control but it does not provide a queryable historical audit trail of every principal who has attempted to modify bucket policies — determining 'who attempted this last month' still requires CloudTrail; conflating the two tools' capabilities into one control misses that they solve genuinely different problems (prevention vs. attribution).
topic: AWS Config provides continuous, automatic evaluation of resource configuration state against compliance rules (with optional auto-remediation), making it the right tool for an ongoing 'must never drift into a non-compliant state' requirement, while CloudTrail records the specific API call events (who called which action, when, from where) making it the right tool for after-the-fact attribution of a specific change. The exam explicitly tests this Config-vs-CloudTrail distinction as one of its highest-yield Domain 4 pairs: Config answers 'was this ever misconfigured and for how long,' CloudTrail answers 'who made the API call that changed it' — and a well-designed scenario, like this one, deliberately asks for both together, mapped correctly to their respective tool.

question: A media streaming company's data engineering team in the EU (operating under an AWS account in eu-west-1) needs to grant a US-based analytics vendor's IAM role, in a completely separate AWS account outside the company's AWS Organization, temporary read access to specific viewership aggregate tables for a 90-day pilot contract, after which access must automatically expire without anyone needing to remember to manually revoke it. The underlying S3 data is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, and the tables are registered in Lake Formation. The legal team also requires that the vendor never be able to access raw, row-level viewership events — only the pre-aggregated, non-personally-identifiable summary tables. What combination of configurations correctly implements this temporary, scoped, auto-expiring cross-account access?
options: Create a permanent IAM user for the vendor with an access key, grant it direct s3:GetObject on the entire data lake bucket, and instruct the vendor to delete the access key themselves after 90 days.

Grant the vendor account's root user full administrative access to the AWS Organization's management account temporarily, since root-level access is the simplest way to grant broad but time-boxed access.
Grant Lake Formation permissions scoped only to the aggregate tables, add a KMS kms:Decrypt grant for the vendor role, and auto-revoke both via a scheduled Lambda after 90 days.
Share the aggregate tables with the vendor by exporting them to a public S3 bucket with no access controls for the duration of the pilot, since public access is easiest to set up and tear down.
explanations: A – Incorrect. A permanent IAM user with long-lived access keys is exactly the anti-pattern the exam treats as wrong for external/temporary access — it grants access to the entire bucket (violating the 'only aggregate tables, never raw events' requirement) and relies on the vendor's own goodwill to self-revoke, which is precisely the kind of manual dependency the requirement wants eliminated.

B – Incorrect. Granting the vendor root-level administrative access to the management account is a massive, wildly disproportionate over-grant that violates least privilege catastrophically and has nothing to do with scoping access to specific aggregate tables — this is a clearly inappropriate answer for a scoped data-sharing scenario.

C – Correct. Lake Formation cross-account grants scoped specifically to the aggregate tables (excluding the raw event tables) satisfy the least-privilege, no-raw-data requirement; the KMS key policy grant is required as the separate, additional layer needed for the vendor to actually decrypt the encrypted S3 objects (the standard cross-account KMS gotcha); and an automated, scheduled revocation mechanism (rather than manual follow-up) ensures both the Lake Formation grant and the KMS key policy statement are programmatically removed at the 90-day mark, guaranteeing access actually expires without depending on anyone remembering — this combination correctly addresses every stated constraint (scoped, cross-account, encrypted, auto-expiring).

D – Incorrect. Publishing the data to a public bucket with no access controls violates the fundamental requirement for scoped, controlled access entirely, exposes the data to anyone on the internet (not just the intended vendor), and provides no mechanism for automatic expiration at all — this fails every stated constraint simultaneously.
topic: Temporary, scoped, cross-account data sharing on AWS-native governed data requires layering several distinct controls: Lake Formation grants scoped to only the specific tables that should be shared (never broader), a corresponding KMS key policy grant enabling the receiving account's principal to decrypt the underlying encrypted objects (the classic cross-account encryption two-layer requirement), and — since neither Lake Formation grants nor KMS key policy statements expire on their own — an explicit automated mechanism (scheduled Lambda/Step Functions) to revoke both at the intended expiration time, since there's no native 'auto-expiring grant' primitive to rely on passively. The exam-pattern trigger combining 'temporary access,' 'cross-account,' 'KMS-encrypted,' and 'must not require manual revocation' requires recognizing and correctly combining all three of these layers rather than any single one alone.
